newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends lower as mark stages European rally.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends lower as mark stages European rally.

text.p: The dollar fell to a two-week low against the German mark Monday as investors dumped most European currencies in favour of the relative safety of the German unit.

Various reports of weakening European resolve to cut bloated government spending to unite under a single currency triggered waves of mark buying, both against European units and the dollar, market players said.
"There seemed to have been great demand for marks," said Jay Wertheimer, senior foreign exchange trader at Banco di Sicilia in New York.

A surprise announcement that France would hold parliamentary elections at the end of May cast doubts on France's commitment to slashing its government debt in preparation for a proposed single European currency in 1999.
Meanwhile, the International Monetary Fund warned that Italy needed large cuts in its own government spending to qualify for the single currency and European Monetary Union.

The mark is traditionally viewed as a stronger currency than the French franc and Italian lira. Any sign that the proposed union of the mark with the weaker units is in jeopardy typically prompts investors to switch into marks.
"We saw broad-based mark buying against the French franc, the lira, the Spanish peseta and (Japanese) yen, said Audrey McNiff, a vice president for foreign exchange sales at Goldman Sachs.
French President Jacques Chirac surprised the market by calling for an election on May 25 and June 1, nine months ahead of schedule, and likened it to a referendum on EMU.
Later in U.S. trade, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said a delay in EMU was possible if "big countries" fail to meet the entry requirements.
EMU calls for participants to reduce their annual federal budget deficits to 3 percent of gross domestic product -- a goal most European nations currently fail to meet.
The dollar closed at 1.6965 marks, down from 1.7118 late Friday, and 125.30 yen, down from 125.89.
The U.S. currency also fell against the Swiss franc to 1.4410 from 1.4573 Friday. The British pound rose to $1.6362 from $1.6340. The dollar edged higher to Canadian $1.3989 from C$1.3998.
Despite the surge in mark buying, dealers said the dollar would likely rebound in coming sessions, since the weakness of European currencies ultimately has little to do with the dollar.
"We got a lot of follow-through on the whole EMU situation, but I'm not 100 percent convinced that sentiment has changed on the dollar," said Wertheimer.
Investors lightened up on dollar holdings versus the yen ahead of a meeting of global economic officials on Sunday April 27.

Economic leaders of the Group of Seven industrial nations, or G7, will meet in Washington on Sunday, and market players were wary of official statements or actions to stop the dollar's meteoric rise against the yen.
"The bears are looking for a downtick in the dollar going into the G7 and waiting to see how bold that move is," said Greg Perman, chief currency dealer at Credit Commerciale de France in New York.
